title: VACATION RACES
subtitle: Data Science Insights — the national-park destination runner: who they are, where they are, and how to reach them.
prepared: Prepared for Vacation Races  ·  Genomic Digital  ·  September 2026
objective:
Vacation Races sells a finish line inside a national park: cupless half marathons and trail festivals at Zion, Bryce Canyon, the Grand Canyon, Yosemite, Grand Teton, Yellowstone, Glacier, Rocky Mountain, the Great Smoky Mountains and Acadia, and an international calendar that now includes Iceland. The purchase is a trip before it is a race — flights, a rental car, three nights near a park gate — and the buyer is very often booking for a couple or a group of friends, not for herself alone.

The goal of this work is to define that audience so it can be bought: to describe, with statistical confidence, what the people who search for Vacation Races' events also search for, drive, wear, watch and read, and where in the country they are — and to separate the destination runner cleanly from the two populations that sit next to her in search: the general national-park tourist, and the local road racer.

Genomic Digital's Heimdall platform was used to build the segment from Vacation Races' own race vocabulary, correlate it against TBD million phrases of American search behaviour, and isolate the clusters that matter for strategy, creative and media placement.
agenda: How Heimdall builds an audience from language, and why the race phrases — not the park names — had to be the seeds
The destination-runner definition, its geography, and fourteen correlation categories read from the data
Roles that should not be collapsed: the series collector who returns, and the once-a-year trip runner who books for the group
Value proposition, creative hooks, channel guidance and campaign structure
method_steps: Start from Vacation Races' own vocabulary: the brand, each race name as it is searched (zion half marathon, yosemite half marathon, grand teton half marathon …), the trail festivals, and the category phrase 'national park half marathon'. Measure which carry real US search volume; the top TBD terms carry TBD% of it and form the core.

Every phrase in the corpus carries a geo-spatial fingerprint — how its search interest distributes across the 51 states, 210 DMAs, countries and congressional districts. The segment's fingerprint is the signed combination of its seed phrases.

The segment is correlated against every one of TBD million phrases and TBD anchor columns in the Heimdall Matrix — public search behaviour, not a panel and not a survey. Every number in this deck is one of those correlations.

TBD named entities — parks, races, airlines, hotel brands, cars, retailers, media — are read against the segment by hand, category by category, and only the clusters that survive scrutiny are reported.
corpus_blurb: Heimdall is a correlation engine over language. Each phrase people search is a row; each anchor an advertiser might buy against is a column; the cell is how closely their geographic search behaviour moves together. An audience is a signed formula over rows — positives added, competing senses subtracted — and every chart in this deck is that formula read down one category of named entities.

senses_blurb:
A national park's name is not owned by the race that runs through it. In US search, 'yellowstone' is first a television drama, then a park; 'acadia' is first a GMC SUV; 'grand canyon' is, in several states, a university before it is a canyon; 'zion' is a basketball player and a scripture before it is a trailhead. Seeding the segment from park names would therefore build an audience of television viewers, SUV shoppers and online-degree applicants.

The segment is instead declared from the race phrases themselves — 'zion half marathon', 'yosemite half marathon' — which are specific, and the competing senses that the semantic probe finds nearby are subtracted explicitly. That is the same device our Ragnar Races work used to subtract the Viking from the relay, and our TAB Bank work used to subtract job-seekers from a bank's customer pole.

strengths: No panel, no questionnaire, no audience framing by the researcher. The method reads what people actually search, where, and lets the correlations surface the clusters.

The segment is built from Vacation Races' race names as people type them, not from a generic 'runner' or 'national park visitor' proxy — and the park-name senses that would pollute it are kept out by construction.
Every figure is a correlation in the live Heimdall Matrix, reproducible on demand, and the segment now exists as a permanent column that can be re-read as the corpus grows — race by race, if wanted.
limitations: Correlation over geography says who searches alongside whom, not why. Turning the clusters into strategy takes judgement, and this deck says where it is exercising it.
The correlations are small in absolute terms (a destination half marathon is a small population). Read sign, ordering and distance from the average band — not the decimal.

Age, income, household composition and gender were not scored in this pass. Vacation Races' own registration data (gender split, repeat rate, home ZIPs) outranks any correlation here and should be laid beside it.
segment_section_blurb: The definition, its geography, and fourteen correlation categories — each read against named entities, with the average American searcher as the reference band.
segment_def_blurb:
TBD terms carry more than TBD% of Vacation Races' US search volume, so the segment is built from them. A longer twelve-seed definition (adding every race on the calendar and the trail festivals) was also built and measured; TBD — expected: it reads the same clusters with more noise, because low-volume race names carry noisy fingerprints and equal votes.

The formula is Heimdall's grammar: the same one our Ragnar pole used to subtract 'ragnar lothbrok'.

segment_formula.text: + zn( yosemite half marathon )        TBD / mo
+ zn( grand teton half marathon )     TBD / mo
+ zn( grand canyon half marathon )    TBD / mo
- zn( TBD collision, if confirmed )*0.5     TBD / mo   <- TBD sense
correlation with any phrase = Heimdall h

categories_blurb: Each category is a hand-built list of named entities — national parks and gateway towns, destination races, airlines and hotel brands, cars, retailers, streaming services, news outlets — read against the segment. The chart plots every entity by its correlation with the destination-runner segment (vertical), its political lean (horizontal) and its US search volume (size). The grey band is the average entity; anything above it is over-indexed for this audience.
geo_blurb: The segment's search fingerprint by state, standardised. Positive means Vacation Races' events are searched more than the national rate; negative, less. This is the client's own footprint read from the corpus — not a lookalike.

DRIVE-TIME RADIUS OF THE PARKS
geo_insight:
TBD from geomap_states.json. Expected shape, to confirm or correct: Utah leads (St George headquarters, Zion and Bryce), with Nevada (Las Vegas is Zion's airport), Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Wyoming and Montana behind it — the Intermountain West that can drive to a start line. California, Washington and Oregon follow for Yosemite and the western calendar. If Tennessee, North Carolina or Maine appear, the Smokies and Acadia races are pulling weight and the seed set is balanced; if they do not, the eastern races are under-represented in the seeds and the insight must say so.

The under-index is expected to be the large-population states without a park on the calendar and without a cheap flight to one: TBD.

Two implications to test against the real map: (1) the audience is regional to the parks and follows the calendar, so always-on spend should weight the park footprint and its drive-time radius, not population; (2) the largest under-indexed states are the fly-in destination-race prospects — the market list for a 'make it a vacation' campaign.
persona_section_blurb: Roles, deliberately not collapsed. The collector comes back every year for the next park; the trip runner books once, for the group, and decides where everyone sleeps.

appendix_reading: Vertical axis: Heimdall h — the correlation between the entity's geographic search fingerprint and the Vacation Races destination-runner segment column. Above the grey band = over-indexed for this audience.
Horizontal axis: political spectrum — the entity's correlation with a Republican audience column minus a Democratic one. The centre band is neutral.
Bubble size: US monthly search volume for the entity (log scale).
Amber points are the five strongest entities in the category; dark grey the three weakest. Labels are the search phrase as it exists in the corpus.
Entities missing from the corpus were substituted with their nearest real search phrase or dropped; every substitution is listed in the working file.
